selectionPolicy.cadence: Daily refresh; a new review is published when a fresh primary paper clears the selection gate.
selectionPolicy.selection: The selector favors primary papers with strong fit for agents, computer vision, retrieval, reasoning, representation learning, and deployable ML systems.
selectionPolicy.writing: Reviews are original English editorial notes. Abstracts and third-party commentary are used for triage only and are not republished.

reviewSourceWatch.label: Yannic Kilcher / CVPR source watch
reviewSourceWatch.note: Track Yannic Kilcher public paper-analysis sources alongside official CVPR/CVF sources. Do not claim a specific Yannic CVPR review unless a public source ledger confirms it.

reviews.title: Can AI Agents Synthesize Scientific Conclusions?
reviews.dek: A paper worth reading for the traces, not the demo: how agents communicate, monitor, or expose state when the run gets long.
reviews.selectionReason: Selected from primary ML research feeds because it is recent, source-linked, and has a clear implementation question for agents, CV, retrieval, reasoning, or ML systems.
reviews.editorVerdict: The useful question is not whether the agent looks smart in a demo; it is whether its state, messages, and failure modes can be inspected after the run is over.
reviews.whatItClaims: Can AI Agents Synthesize Scientific Conclusions? argues that agent quality depends on the communication or monitoring substrate around the model, not only on the base model's raw ability.
reviews.technicalHinge: The hinge is observability. If the proposed communication or monitoring state cannot be replayed, inspected, and scored, it will be hard to trust once agents run for minutes instead of turns.
reviews.productionAngle: Try to turn the method into a trace contract: every action should leave behind state, evidence, and a reason a reviewer can accept or reject.
reviews.skepticism: This is a triage review from cs.AI, cs.CL, not a reproduction. I would not use the result until code, data conditions, ablations, and failure examples are checked against a task I actually need.
readingPath: Read the method before the benchmark table.
Find the ablation that removes the claimed mechanism.
Write one product failure case the paper should survive.

reviews.title: I Know What You Meme, Even If it Emerged Today: Understanding Evolving Memes through Open-World Knowledge Acquisition
reviews.dek: A multimodal paper to read through failure cases: what the model can verify, where it hallucinates, and what a user can inspect.
reviews.selectionReason: Selected because the paper has a primary source link and a clear implementation question for agents, CV, retrieval, reasoning, or ML systems.
reviews.editorVerdict: The paper matters if it changes what the system can verify about an image or video, not just what the model can caption after the fact.
reviews.whatItClaims: I Know What You Meme, Even If it Emerged Today: Understanding Evolving Memes through Open-World Knowledge Acquisition pushes on visual understanding where the important output is not a fluent caption, but a model behavior that can be inspected against the underlying scene.
reviews.technicalHinge: The hinge is whether the method aligns visual evidence with the answer path. A model that only produces a polished answer still needs a separate gate for groundedness.
reviews.productionAngle: Build a failure gallery before a demo gallery: occlusion, domain shift, ambiguous prompts, and outputs that look plausible but are wrong.
reviews.skepticism: This is a triage review from cs.AI, not a reproduction. I would not use the result until code, data conditions, ablations, and failure examples are checked against a task I actually need.

reviews.title: Entity-Centric World Models: Interaction-Aware Masking for Causal Video Prediction
reviews.dek: A JEPA-style physical-AI paper to read for the hard part: whether video prediction learns object state, contact, and causal motion rather than polished pixels.
reviews.selectionReason: Selected because the paper has a primary source link and a clear implementation question for agents, CV, retrieval, reasoning, or ML systems.
reviews.editorVerdict: The useful question is whether JEPA-style prediction changes representation around physical events. If the embedding stays calm when objects touch, separate, occlude, or change trajectory, it is not yet a world model for builders.
reviews.whatItClaims: Entity-Centric World Models argues that standard patch masking can make JEPA-like video objectives miss rare but important kinematic events, and proposes interaction-aware masking to push learning toward objects and causal motion.
reviews.technicalHinge: The hinge is the mask policy. It has to expose the moments where the physical system actually changes: contact, identity, occlusion, relative motion, and state transitions. Otherwise the model can still optimize for texture continuity.
reviews.productionAngle: Before putting this into a robotics or physical-AI prototype, build a failure set around object handoffs, near-collisions, hidden state, and grasp/no-grasp transitions. Score whether the representation predicts the event, not only the next frame.
reviews.skepticism: This is a triage review from cs.CV, not a reproduction. I would want code, ablations for the masking strategy, object-tracking error analysis, and tests on real robot or egocentric video before treating it as a deployable physical-AI component.
readingPath: Start with the masking objective and ask what physical event it forces the model to care about.
Check whether the evaluation separates visual smoothness from causal state prediction.
Look for ablations where interaction-aware masking is removed or replaced with random patch masking.

reviews.title: UltraVR: A Diagnostic Ultra-Resolution Image-VQA Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Reasoning
reviews.dek: A fresh computer-vision review for high-resolution VQA: can the model find tiny, distant evidence, or does it answer from priors and captions?
reviews.selectionReason: Selected because the paper has a primary source link and a clear implementation question for agents, CV, retrieval, reasoning, or ML systems.
reviews.editorVerdict: This is the right kind of CV benchmark to watch: it makes the model earn an answer by finding small evidence at scale. Final-answer accuracy is not enough when the relevant pixels are tiny, far apart, or easy to skip.
reviews.whatItClaims: UltraVR evaluates ultra-resolution image VQA where the answer depends on subtle or spatially distributed visual evidence, pushing beyond benchmarks that only check whether the final answer sounds plausible.
reviews.technicalHinge: The hinge is evidence routing. A useful system has to crop, retrieve, or attend to the decisive regions before reasoning. If the model cannot expose what visual evidence it used, the answer is hard to trust in inspection workflows.
reviews.productionAngle: Use it as a release-gate shape for OCR, floor-plan review, medical imaging triage, satellite inspection, and catalog matching: require the model to return the answer plus the supporting crop or coordinate evidence.
reviews.skepticism: This is a triage review from cs.CV, not a reproduction. I would check data overlap, image resolution handling, evidence annotations, and whether strong baselines fail because of reasoning or because of image tiling and compression.
readingPath: Read the task construction before the headline model table.
Check whether evidence localization is evaluated separately from answer accuracy.
Map one benchmark task to a real inspection workflow and define the required proof artifact.
